title: How much? The amount of chemical change
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: R2.1#c10 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.1#c09 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.1#c11 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.1#c12 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: R2.1#q07, R2.1#q09, R2.1#q12, R2.1#q08, R2.1#q10, R2.1#q13, R2.1#q11, R2.1#q14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Excess reactant
items.clue: Some of it is left over at the end.

items.label: Limiting reactant
items.clue: Completely used up, so it fixes the maximum amount of product.

items.label: Theoretical yield
items.clue: The maximum amount of product that could be obtained, by calculation.

items.label: Experimental yield
items.clue: The mass (or amount) of product actually obtained in a practical preparation.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the theoretical yield of a product in a reaction?

options.text: The mass of product actually obtained at the end of the experiment
The total mass of all the reactants put in, since mass is conserved
The mass of product calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant
The mass of product calculated from the reactant with the smaller number of moles

questions.explanation: The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product, calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant using the mole ratio and assuming complete reaction with no losses.

questions.stem: A student heats 2.70 g of aluminium in 8.51 g of chlorine and collects 7.60 g of aluminium chloride: 2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2AlCl₃(s). What is the percentage yield of aluminium chloride? A_r: Al 26.98; Cl 35.45
questions.explanation: n(Al) = 0.1001 mol and n(Cl₂) = 0.1200 mol. Al would need 1.5 × 0.1001 = 0.1501 mol Cl₂, so Cl₂ is limiting. n(AlCl₃) = 0.1200 × 2/3 = 0.08002 mol, theoretical yield = 0.08002 × 133.33 = 10.67 g, and percentage yield = 7.60 ÷ 10.67 × 100 = 71.2%.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is manufactured by reacting methane with steam: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). In one batch, 16.0 kg of methane gave 4.80 kg of hydrogen. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen by this reaction? A_r: H 1.01; C 12.01; O 16.00
questions.explanation: Atom economy = M_r(desired product) ÷ ΣM_r(all reactants) × 100, using the coefficients: 3 × 2.02 ÷ (16.05 + 18.02) × 100 = 6.06 ÷ 34.07 × 100 = 17.8%. The rest of the mass ends up as the by-product CO.

questions.stem: A student heats 4.86 g of magnesium with 4.00 g of oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). Which statement about the limiting reactant is correct? A_r: O 16.00; Mg 24.31

options.text: Magnesium is limiting: 0.200 mol Mg needs 0.100 mol O₂, and 0.125 mol is present.
Oxygen is limiting, because a smaller mass of oxygen than of magnesium is present.
Oxygen is limiting, because there is only 0.125 mol of O₂ but 0.200 mol of Mg present.
Magnesium is limiting: 4.86 g Mg needs only 2.43 g O₂, and 4.00 g is present.

questions.explanation: n(Mg) = 4.86 ÷ 24.31 = 0.200 mol and n(O₂) = 4.00 ÷ 32.00 = 0.125 mol. The 2 : 1 ratio means 0.200 mol Mg needs only 0.100 mol O₂, so oxygen is in excess (0.025 mol left) and magnesium is limiting.

questions.stem: A student prepares a solid product, filters it off and weighs it. The theoretical yield was calculated correctly from the limiting reactant, but the percentage yield comes out as 108%. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The product was weighed before it had been completely dried.
A catalyst was present, and it increased the mass of product formed.
The excess reactant formed more product after the limiting one ran out.
The reaction ran more efficiently than usual and beat its expected yield.

questions.explanation: The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product the limiting reactant can form, so a yield above 100% means that the solid weighed was not pure product. Water left in an undried solid adds mass and is the usual cause.

questions.stem: Which statement about atom economy and waste in an industrial process is correct?

options.text: The higher the percentage yield, the higher the atom economy, so less waste is produced.
Atom economy counts one molecule of each substance, so the coefficients do not affect it.
A process with an atom economy of 100% produces no waste of any kind at all.
The lower the atom economy, the greater the proportion of reactant mass that becomes waste.

questions.explanation: Atom economy is the percentage of the total mass of reactants that can end up in the desired product. The rest ends up in by-products, so as atom economy falls, the proportion of the reactant mass converted to waste rises: the two are inversely related.

questions.stem: 5.00 cm³ of propane is mixed with 40.0 cm³ of oxygen and ignited, and the propane burns completely: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. The mixture is then cooled to the original room temperature and pressure. What is the total volume of gas present at the end?

options.text: 50.0 cm³
30.0 cm³
45.0 cm³
15.0 cm³

questions.explanation: 5.00 cm³ C₃H₈ uses 5 × 5.00 = 25.0 cm³ O₂, so 15.0 cm³ O₂ is left over, and it forms 3 × 5.00 = 15.0 cm³ CO₂. At room temperature the water is a liquid. Total gas = 15.0 + 15.0 = 30.0 cm³.

questions.stem: Ethanol is manufactured either by fermentation, C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g), or by hydration of ethene, C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g). Which statement about the two routes is correct? A_r: H 1.01; C 12.01; O 16.00

options.text: A higher percentage yield in fermentation would raise its atom economy closer to hydration's.
Fermentation has the lower atom economy, so more of its reactant mass becomes by-product.
Hydration has an atom economy of 100%, so a hydration plant produces no waste of any kind.
Only about a quarter of the reactant mass in fermentation ends up in ethanol (atom economy 25.6%).
